title: Knowing When to Stop: Adaptive Sampling for LLM Evals
hook: Most evals run every item the same number of times, long after the estimate has stopped moving. Treat it as sequential measurement instead and 57–97% of those trials turn out to be unnecessary.
key_points: Fixed sampling budgets keep re-testing items whose scores are already precise.
optstop reframes evaluation as sequential measurement: sample where uncertainty is high, stop where it isn't.
Built on hierarchical Bayesian inference; supports binary, ordinal, and continuous outcomes.
Every benchmark item stays eligible for sampling — no pre-calibrated item bank required.
A safeguard samples more cautiously near zero performance, where rare successes carry the most information.
In a 200-item, 10-epoch illustration it removed 57–97% of planned trials with equivalent overall conclusions.
content_html: Running an eval usually means picking a number — ten samples per item, say — and applying it uniformly. But items differ. Some settle after two samples; others stay genuinely uncertain after twenty. A fixed budget spends the same compute on both. optstop reframes evaluation as a sequential measurement problem: keep sampling where uncertainty remains high, stop where estimates are precise or stable enough.
extra_html:
How it works

The framework builds on hierarchical Bayesian inference and handles binary, ordinal, and continuous outcomes. Two design choices make it practical. Every benchmark item stays eligible for sampling throughout, so it doesn't require a pre-calibrated item bank the way item-response-theory approaches often do. And it includes a safeguard that samples more cautiously as measured performance approaches zero — the regime where a single rare success carries the most information and stopping early would be most misleading. It runs live during an evaluation or retrospectively over logged results.

The savings

In an illustrative 200-item, 10-epoch evaluation, the framework removed 57%–97% of planned trials across nine validation settings while reaching overall conclusions equivalent to the full run. The size of the saving depends heavily on evaluation design — but the general point holds: eval compute can be allocated by uncertainty rather than by fixed repetition counts, and the second policy is rarely the efficient one.

related.title: Can We Trust Item Response Theory for AI Evaluation?
related.hook: IRT ranks models off a handful of items instead of averaging accuracy — but the math was built for human test-takers, and AI benchmarks break its assumptions in ways that quietly distort rankings.

related.title: Who Thinks Best Depends on How Long You Let Them
related.hook: Change the token budget and the leaderboard changes with it. Model rankings reversed on every benchmark tested — which means a single-budget eval is measuring the budget as much as the model.

related.title: Do Agent Benchmarks Measure Capability?
related.hook: An agent score only means something if the task still requires the skill it claims to test. Auditing 2,385 traces, two-thirds showed the agent taking a shortcut instead.

flashcards.prompt: What is wasteful about a fixed sampling budget in LLM evaluation?
flashcards.back_html: It tests every item the same number of times even after that item's estimate is already precise — spending compute where there's no remaining uncertainty to resolve.

flashcards.prompt: What safeguard does optstop apply as measured performance approaches zero?

choices.text: It samples more cautiously there, because rare successes matter most
It stops sampling immediately to save budget
It switches the outcome model from binary to continuous

flashcards.explanation_html: Near-zero performance is exactly where a single rare success would change the conclusion, so the framework keeps sampling more cautiously rather than stopping early.

flashcards.prompt: What did the illustrative 200-item, 10-epoch evaluation show?

choices.text: 57–97% of planned trials removed across nine validation settings, with equivalent overall conclusions
A 2x speedup but with materially different rankings
Savings only on items the model answered correctly every time

flashcards.explanation_html: Across nine validation settings the framework removed 57%–97% of planned trials while reaching conclusions equivalent to the full run.
